extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, legal practitioners, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts core legal doctrines and evaluative standards used in assessing patentability, claim drafting/construction, infringement, remedies, and procedural rights in U.S. patent practice. Covers tests for combinations/compositions, disclosure requirements, conception/reduction-to-practice, co-ownership, damages, jurisdiction, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class of Objects — description must serve purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of class of objects improper unless each object will answer the purpose
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index reference notes (496 n.1; 497 n.2; 50011.1). Implicit criterion: when describing a class of objects in a specification, each object described should have a purpose/utility relevant to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical errors in letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Letters-Patent. (Index references 637-639). Indicates treatise guidance on treating/correcting clerical errors in issued patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination — definition and essential qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination defined; essential qualities of a combination; a combination is an entirety whose essence and existence depend on what it produces and how elements co-operate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries: defined (163,156 n.2,277), essential qualities (277,281), an entirety (155 n.2), essence and existence depend on what (155 n.2), a new means essentially distinct from its elements (155), belongs to same class of inventions as its elements (166 n.2). Tests: not patentable unless the result of inventive skill; not an aggregation — distinguished by nature of result; must produce a new result; producing new result must be new. See also nature of inventive act (155 n.8), elements of a combination, identity of elements, cooperative law, and subcombinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination — identity, equivalents, and variation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of elements and cooperative law determine whether a combination is the same as prior art; equivalents and variation of elements governed by peculiar rules
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index notes: identity of elements alone is not necessarily determinative; use of new element in a combination may create a new combination; equivalents treated specially (879,882 n.1); rules same whether elements are old or new; special rules for chemical vs mechanical combinations; divergences by shape, proportions, arrangement, use, etc. Consider identity of subcombinations and when improvements amount to a substantial change rather than mere improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for combinations — scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules concerning claims directed to combinations: what a claim for a combination covers and limits on coverage
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index guidance: Claim for (524,525). Key points: does not cover its elements; cannot cover elements already patented; elements not claimed are regarded as old; elements claimed thereby become essential; claims not withdrawn by disclaimer; not declared unessential by the courts; regarded as material by inventor so held against transferees; covers the exact union of the exact elements; joinder of subcombinations and elements; what acts infringe; use of less than all elements (references 888,928); defenses must apply to entire combination (1026 n.3); anticipated when (282ii.8); not anticipated by prior use of elements (318 n.1). Also relates to identity of arts, omission/alteration of essential steps, and distinctions for machines vs manufactures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction (claim interpretation) — general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of patents (claims and specification) — how words are applied to subject matter and how patents are interpreted by courts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index entries: Construction defined as part of inventive act; measures the monopoly; may be made by court or jury; often treated as matter of law; liberal in favor of patentee; cannot depart from or cure defects in language; must tend to clear definition of the invention; not alternative to render claim elastic or ambiguous; should be consistent with real nature of the invention if possible; actual character of invention may be shown; names given to inventions construed by persons skilled in the art; entire patent construed together; description construed with other parts of specification; claims govern when clear; description used if claims ambiguous; general words limited by nature of invention; extrinsic evidence (parol) admissible in certain circumstances; expert evidence may aid; construction is liberal on questions of joinder; later patents not construed to cover earlier if avoidable; arrangement of words unimportant; words mean what applicant intended; words take meaning they had at date of invention; general limited and special extended when necessary; construed by correspondence with Patent Office; ambiguous language may be rejected as surplusage; pioneer patents broadly construed; re-issue construed by original; construction applied to combinations, improvements, joint inventions, etc. Also: make all claimed elements material; construction for principle, function, effect; aid of drawings and model; words and special phrases (e.g., 'substantially as described', 'generic') treated specially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness in Description
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index reference 491. Implies requirement that the specification must be complete enough to satisfy statutory/constructive tests (e.g., enablement/adequate disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition — definition, unity, and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition defined; essential attributes and how composition differs from its elements and mode of intermixture
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index entries: Composition defined 192; essential attributes 195; composition is a true combination (193), distinct from elements and mode of intermixture (194); character determined by analysis (801); intermixture of ingredients (192); no special substance or mode of intermixture essential (194); unit and unity destroyed by additions/omissions (196); identity of composition determined by identity of ingredients, combination, and properties. Additional rules: identical however produced (197); natural vs artificial (197); equivalents governed by special rule; improvement in composition; removal of defects; reducible to practice in many forms and all covered by patent (199); not patentable until reduced to practice (198). Description and claim guidance: description in patent (500); claim for composition (532) covers only equivalent ingredients (514), requires neither model nor drawing (549), joinder with ingredients/process/apparatus (476); infringement rules applicable (1928).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceiver vs Reducer (true inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceiver, not reducer, is the true inventor; earliest conceiver may be later reducer and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index references 875 n.1; 373. Links to Conception, Reduction to Practice, Priority, and Interferences. Criterion affects who is entitled to the patent where conception and reduction-to-practice differ among parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception — definition and evidentiary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception of an invention defined; complete conception generates an idea of practically operative means and is complete when ready for reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries: defined (376-382,876); not reduced to practice is not an invention (875 a.8); conception differs from embodied conception; conception generates idea of means (377); suggestion of an end without means is not conception; complete when ready for reduction (379); experiment is not conception (379 n.1); date of conception is date of complete conception (380); may be shown on priority questions; may be contemporaneous with or precede reduction; how proved; joint invention date; foreign invention date in U.S. See also Conceiver, Date, Delay, Diligence, Interferences, Inventor, Priority, Reduction to Practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-operating inventors and co-owners — definitions and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-operating inventors defined; co-owners of patents and their rights, duties, and liabilities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-operating inventors: defined (892-895,866,392); conceivers of separable and united ideas; suggestion-only as to mode of reduction not co-inventor. Co-owners: may be any number (795 n.1); how created; relations between (795); not co-partners; have distinct interests; monopoly resides indivisibly in all; each controls his own right and can grant/license under it; license or assignment by one is good against all (796 n.1); not accountable to each other for use; reciprocal rights and duties; liability to account to each other for profits; issue of patent to one enures to benefit of all; not estopped to deny validity as against each other; measure of liability for infringement by co-owner; damages distribution; contracts and partnership relations among co-owners; when agreements are within statute of frauds (or not). See related doctrines (assignments, estoppel, re-issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies and evidentiary effect of patents/specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of patents, etc., as evidence; copies from Patent Office as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index: copies of patents as evidence (1015); copies of recorded patents how made (627); copies of specifications only do not show that the invention was patented (1027 n.5); errors in copies from Patent Office how corrected (627 a.4); copies are prima facie evidence originals genuine (1040).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction — interpretation of special words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: How special words and commonly used patent phrases are interpreted in construction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index references to interpretation of foreign phrases, 'substantially as described,' 'generic,' 'specification,' 'manufacture' (750); special words interpreted (751); phrases of degree e.g., 'in any convenient manner,' 'suitable materials,' 'making,' 'selling,' 'use,' 'jointly' discussed (761). Construction may be influenced by acquiescence and correspondence with Patent Office; requires more than a year in some contexts; see also guidance on parol evidence and finality in particular administrative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court powers and jurisdiction in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts' powers to interpret, review, and adjudicate patent rights; jurisdictional rules for federal and state courts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index entries: courts interpret patents and may refuse evidence to aid; can decide sufficiency of claim as matter of law; ambiguity usually for jury; Supreme Court construction is final; courts may declare patent void if description insufficient on its face. Federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over cases arising under Patent Law to secure uniformity; jurisdiction conferred to Circuit and Supreme Court issues; State court jurisdiction limited/affected; court powers regarding appeals, mandamus, and finality of Patent Office decisions discussed. See related topics: Court of Claims, federal/state jurisdictional distinctions, remedies, contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for infringement — measure and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for measuring damages in actions at law and in equity for patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index summary: Damages in actions at law (1049-1071); implied from infringement; not synonymous with profits; liberal doctrine in American law; assessed irrespective of parties' financial condition; remote/consequential damages generally not allowable; nominal damages occasions; burden of proof on plaintiff; plaintiff's evidence liberally construed; license fee as measure in some cases; measure depends on plaintiff's mode of exploiting invention (use/sale); defendant's profits may guide measurement; value at date of infringement relevant; special rules for improvements, partial infringement, making-only cases; interest, trebling, counsel fees considerations (treble in court discretion; counsel fees sometimes covered). Also allocation among co-owners, proof requirements, and limits (cannot exceed amount claimed in declaration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in applying for patent — legal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of delay in applying for a patent on rights, abandonment, and priority
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index notes: delay in applying (351 n.2) not ipso facto abandonment to the public; does not make the invention a lost art; effect on rights of prior inventor (388-390); may estop first inventor from claiming against later rival if delay is unreasonable; after application, delay not abandonment if unavoidable; in Patent Office delay cannot prejudice inventor; in disclaimers, delay forfeits right (646); in re-issue, unreasonable delay may show original abandonment; 'unavoidable' defined (578 a.2). See related doctrines: abandoned experiment, diligence, laches, re-issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and Claim — both essential and must correspond
rubrics_metrics.description: Both description and claim are essential to a patent and must correspond; claim controls when inconsistent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index entries: DESCRIPTION AND CLAIM both essential to patent (482 a.1); distinct (515 n.1); how written (539); must correspond (515); if inconsistent, claim controls (515 n.1); contradictory description and claim may render both void (515 n.1). Also related: describing and not claiming may constitute abandonment in some circumstances (see 'Describing and not claiming').

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant / prior patent as evidence and defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal effects of defendant's own patent and available defenses in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index: defendant's patent admissible in evidence (1027 n.2), prima facie evidence of novelty and utility but validity not in issue (1041 n.18-19); disclaimers in defendant's patent may estop him; prior pending patents may not be a defense; suppression of evidence, concealment, and estoppel consequences discussed; good faith generally not a defense to infringement; defences must be examined as to profits and books in equity. See entries on specific defenses and estoppel.
